strengths: This paper introduces a communication protocol to explain how the brain has been triggered, the entire process is fluent and reasonable.
The content of the pre-research is sufficient.
The strategy of the prompt is meaningful.
The paper does a good job of motivating and explaining the problem, as well as providing all the necessary details and motivation to understand the necessary background.
The paper focuses on an interesting aspect of generative AI and how it can be used to generate ad creatives with the goal of increasing click-through rates that, over the years, have been declining.
This work has the potential to inform various interested stakeholders, including advertisers, policymakers, and social media operators.
The paper’s approach aims to leverage the power of Generative AI (particularly ChatGPT) to generate content based on principles obtained from the neuroscience field.
Overall, this is an interesting paper on a topic which is of interest to ICLR Conference.
It offers valuable insights into the application of neuroscientifically designed content to enhance ad click-through rates.
The paper astutely recognizes the promise of leveraging Generative AI for this purpose.
The author thoughtfully presents four distinct prompt strategies and supports them with well-structured experiments, thus substantiating the validity of their approach.
weaknesses: The theme of this paper may not be closely related to the conference, as it is only an engineering specification and lacks theoretical explanation.
The presentation of the paper is chaotic, making it difficult to read.

The method mentioned in the paper, which utilizes ChatGTP to generate accurate prompts and generates high-quality digital advertisements using this prompts and a large text-to-image model, has been widely applied in the engineering field and therefore lacks innovation.
This work is too simple, just using the existing GenAI to produce the context and comparing it with the corresponding items.
The prompt is hand-crafted, and cannot be applied flexibly.
The number of samples in the experiment is too small, and the experiments should cover more scenarios.
The evaluation is quite limited and simplistic, given that the sample of the recruited participants is biased (the overwhelming majority being from India).
The evaluation focuses on only two products.
The authors should explain and motivate how they perform the user recruitment procedure and the reason why they selected the two products.
Given these limitations, it’s unclear whether the paper’s results are generalizable.

The paper fails to explain how this study is different from previous efforts that aim to understand the use of neuromarketing methods without the use of Generative AI to create the ad creatives, making the novelty of this work unclear.
The paper does not explain how the envisioned framework will be applied in practice, and the evaluation defines a set of prompts that are very specific to the products studied.
It is unclear whether the envisioned framework can be applied in practice without great input and effort from experts who will guide the generation of the ad creatives.
The framework does not account for user personalization, raising questions about how personalization and privacy concerns will be handled.
There are a couple of references listed as Anonymous, when they are not Anonymous, so these should be fixed.
Consider not using pie charts for the evaluation results, given that it is one of the worst visualization methods.
The experiments are limited to a single product tested on a sample of 236 participants, making the scope of experimentation somewhat narrow.
Expanding the experiment set to encompass a more diverse array of products would strengthen the paper's claims.

The manual design of prompts may not be a scalable solution when considering the need for ad design across a vast array of products; further exploration of automated or semi-automated prompt generation methods could enhance practicality.
